title: NEURO-OPHTHALMIC & MEDICAL EMERGENCIES: INTERNAL MEDICINE FOR FRCS
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam covering life-threatening headaches, coma management, meningitis, encephalitis, and status epilepticus. This poster provides a critical diagnostic framework for distinguishing ophthalmic presentations from systemic neurological emergencies.

data.title: NEURO-OPHTHALMIC & MEDICAL EMERGENCIES: INTERNAL MEDICINE FOR FRCS
data.summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam covering life-threatening headaches, coma management, meningitis, encephalitis, and status epilepticus. This poster provides a critical diagnostic framework for distinguishing ophthalmic presentations from systemic neurological emergencies.

sections.title: A. Life- or Vision-Threatening Headache D.D.
content: 1. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Extremely severe headache, stiff neck,  conscious level; rarely, subhyaloid hemorrhages seen on fundus examination, usually from a ruptured aneurysm.
2. Structural abnormality of the brain e.g tumor, aneurysm, AV malformation ( conscious level, signs of  ICT, or neurologic signs during, and often after, the headache episode).
3. Epidural or subdural hematoma (follows head trauma; altered level of consciousness; may produce anisocoria.).
4. Infectious CNS disorder e.g meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess (fever, stiff neck,  conscious level, photophobia, neurologic signs).
5. Giant cell arteritis (GCA): Age >50 years,  ESR & CRP, scalp tenderness, …..etc.
6. Acute angle-closure glaucoma.
7. Ocular ischemic syndrome.
8. Malignant hypertension.
9.  ICT e.g Papilloedema & ICH (headaches usually worse in the morning & worsened by Valsalva).

sections.title: B. Other Headache Etiologies
content: Migraine
Cluster headache
Tension headache
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: headache or periocular pain may precede the herpetic vesicles.
Sinus headache: may be a serious headache in diabetic patients and immunocompromised hosts because mucormycosis may be responsible.
Vertebral artery dissection (neck pain & cerebellar/medullary signs).
Cervical spine disease.
Paget’s disease ( Alk phos).
Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.
Convergence insufficiency & Accomodative spasm.
Drugs e.g nitrates, CCB & Carbon monoxide poisoning.

rows: Brief attacks of severe paroxysmal & sharp pain (like an electric shock) lasting a few seconds; starts in distribution of one division of trigeminal nerve; Normal facial sensation.

Occurs in middle aged men; Severe unilateral headache with periocular pain in 1st division of trigeminal nerve; Lasts hours to weeks before spontaneous resolution; Associated with ipsilateral postganglionic Horner syndrome.

branches: Metabolic: Drugs, poisoning (CO, alcohol), Hypoglycaemia, Hyperglycaemia, Hypoxia, CO2 narcosis (COPD), Septicaemia, Hypothermia, Myxoedema, Addisonian crisis, Hepatic/uraemic encephalopathy
Neurological: Trauma, Infection (meningitis, encephalitis), Tumours, Stroke, Epilepsy

sections.title: Management of Coma
content: 1. Call for help.
2. ABC.
3. Consider intubation if GCS < 8.
4. Stabilize cervical spine.
5. Vital signs monitoring.
6. Level of consciousness (document).
7. Blood glucose in all patients; give 50 mL 50% dextrose IV immediately if presumed hypoglycemia.
8. Control seizures.
9. Consider IV glucose, IV thiamine (alcohol, Wernicke’s encephalopathy), IV naloxone (opiate intoxication) and IV flumazenil (benzodiazepine intoxication if airway compromised).

10. Brief examination: Signs of trauma (haematoma, laceration, fracture); Signs of other diseases (liver disease, DM); Skin (needle marks, cyanosis, pallor); Smell breath (alcohol, hepatic fetor, ketosis, uremia); Meningism, heart/lung, abdomen/rectum; Eye examination; Foci of infection (abscesses); Examine for CNS asymmetry (tone, spontaneous movements, reflexes).

sections.title: Eye Examination in Coma (Critical Ophthalmic Signs)

headers: Findings and Clinical Significance (Do Not Dilate)
rows: In light coma, test fields with visual threat. No blink in 1 field suggests hemianopia & contralateral hemisphere lesion.
Vestibulo-ocular reflex (doll’s head maneuver or ice water calorics).

a) Fixed, dilated: Unilateral (3rd nerve palsy with transtentorial herniation); Bilateral (atropine or barbiturate poisoning). b) Marcus Gunn pupil: ON or chiasm damage, Pituitary Apoplexy. c) Pin point: Unilateral (Horner’s syndrome); Bilateral (pontine haemorrhage, opiate poisoning).
Papilloedma (↑ ICT). Hemorrhage: subhyaloid & subarachnoid in Terson’s syndrome. Signs of other disease e.g HTN and DM.

sections.title: Advanced Coma Care & Investigations
content: Quick history from family, ambulance staff and bystanders.
Investigations: ABG, FBC, CXR, U&E, LFT, toxin screen, ethanol and drug levels, CT and lumbar puncture.
Urine analysis: save first few for drug levels, monitor outflow, check for glucose and ketones.
Mannitol 20% ± hydrocortisone in case of cerebral edema.
Monitor neurological signs and coma scale.
General care of comatosed patients.
Reference: Waleed Badr, FRCS INTERNAL & EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS (GLASG) EXAM 2016 (Page 52-53).

sections.title: Meningitis: Organisms & Features
content: Organisms: Meningococcus, pneumococcus. Less commonly: H. influenza; listeria; CMV; cryptococcus or TB.
Early Features: headache, leg pains, cold hands/feet, abnormal skin colour.
Signs of Meningism: neck stiffness, photophobia, Kernig’s sign (pain + resistance on passive knee extension with hip flexed).
Later Features:  conscious level & coma, Seizures ± focal CNS signs ± opisthotonus, Petechial rash (non blanching), Signs of septicaemia ( capillary refill; DIC; BP ).

sections.title: Meningitis Management Protocol
content: 1. ABC: Adequate ventilation, Oxygenation, Circulation (IV line).
2. Start antibiotics immediately: < 55Y: Cefotaxime 2g/6h slow IV; > 55Y: Cefotaxime + ampicillin 2g/4h IV (for listeria); Aciclovir (if viral encephalitis suspected).
3. If septicaemic signs: Don’t attempt LP; Get help from critical care; Treat shock & monitoring.
4. If meningitic signs: Dexamethasone 4-10 mg/6h IV (avoid if immunocompromised).
5. If signs of  ICP: Take to ITU & don’t do LP. If no shock/ICP signs: do LP.
6. Subsequent therapy: Cefotaxime 2g/8h IVI for 10 days ( dose in renal failure); Maintenance fluids; Isolation for 1st 24h.
7. Investigations: U&E, FBC, LFT, glucose, coagulation, Blood culture, LP (opening pressure , CSF microscopy), CSF PCR, CXR (TB).

sections.title: Encephalitis: A High-Mortality Emergency
content: Organisms: Viral (HSV-1&2, arboviruses, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, measles, mumps, rabies, West Nile, etc.); Non-viral (Bacteria, TB, malaria, lyme, aspergillosis).
Signs: Confusion, coma, seizures, fever, headache, focal neurological signs ± history of travel/bite.
Investigations: CT/MRI (Focal bilateral temporal lobe = HSV; Meningeal enhancement = meningoencephalitis); LP & CSF PCR ( protein/lymphocytes,  glucose); EEG.
Management: Mortality in untreated viral encephalitis is 70%. Symptomatic (phenytoin for seizure); Aciclovir 10 mg/kg/8h IV over 1h for 14 days.

sections.title: Cerebral Abscess
content: Causes: Follows ear, sinus, dental infection; skull fracture; heart disease; endocarditis; bronchiectasis.
Signs: seizures, fever, signs of  ICP & sepsis elsewhere.
Investigations: CT/MRI,  WBC,  ESR.
Management: Referral to neurosurgery; treat source infection + treat  ICP.

content.center: Status Epilepticus (>30min or no intervening consciousness)
branches: Metabolic: Hyper/hypoglycaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypocalcaemia, Liver/Renal failure

sections.title: Status Epilepticus: Management Steps
content: 1. ABC: Maintain airway (remove false teeth, oral/nasal airway, intubate if needed), 100% O2.
2. Circulation: IV access, take blood (U&E, LFT, glucose, ABG, ECG, calcium, toxicology, anticonvulsant levels).
3. Immediate Treatment: Thiamine 250 mg IV (if alcoholism); Glucose 50% 50 mL (if low); IVI Saline (if hypotensive).
4. Control Seizures (Aim < 20min): Lorazepam 2-4 mg slow bolus (repeat in 10min if needed); OR Diazepam 10 mg IV over 2min (repeat 5 mg/min to max 20mg).
5. If fits continue: Phenytoin infusion (18mg/Kg at ≤ 50mg/min) - Monitor BP/ECG (Beware hypotension/bradycardia).
6. If fits continue: Diazepam infusion (100mg in 500mL 5% dextrose at 40 mL/h); Dexamethasone 10 mg IV (if edema/vasculitis).
7. Final Tier: General anesthesia.
8. Post-control: Start oral drugs & Search for cause.
